title: In two public macaque data sets, V2 and IT response spectra did not decay faster than V1 and V4, unlike the mouse visual hierarchy; class invariance increased without spectral compression
abstract: Mouse higher visual areas have response spectra that decay faster (larger power-law exponent alpha) than VISp. We tested whether this holds in macaque, with the same cvPCA and noise-corrected read-out estimators, in two public Brain-Score data sets: Freeman/Ziemba 2013 (102 V1 and 103 V2 single units; 67 naturalistic textures and 68 spectrally matched noise images) and Majaj/Hong 2015 (88 V4 and 168 IT multi-unit sites in 2 monkeys; 3,200 object images). The plan was written before the tests. Intervals are mean +/- 1.96 SD over 200 random half-unit draws. No macaque comparison showed the mouse compression: Delta alpha (higher minus lower area) was -0.08 (-0.25 to 0.08) for V1 to V2 on textures, -0.07 on noise, -0.18 (-0.39 to 0.03) for V4 to IT on varied objects, -0.06 in one monkey, and -0.28 (-0.46 to -0.11) on objects without pose variation. With the mouse within-animal estimator (30 units, ranks 2-15; mouse natural scenes +0.14, 0.10 to 0.19), all 5 macaque points were below 0, and 66 of 72 robustness estimates were below 0 with none above 0. The share of reliable variance between texture families or objects rose from V1 to V2 (0.26 to 0.36; also for noise) and from V4 to IT (0.12 to 0.26), so invariance increased without compression. This rejects the account that invariance steepens spectra. IT was only partly a linear V4 read-out (ratio 0.37 against 0.56 in reverse), but in one monkey both directions were equal (0.22, 0.24). Limits: small public samples (29-51 units per draw), the 30 % public FZ split, multi-unit V4/IT sites, different stimuli across species, and exploratory robustness and cross-species contrasts.

display.caption: Spectral decay across the hierarchy. (a) Mean cvPCA spectra of 51 V1 and 51 V2 units for naturalistic textures (Freeman/Ziemba 2013). (b) Mean spectra of 44 V4 and 44 IT sites for 1,280 varied object images per draw (Majaj/Hong 2015). Grey: alpha fit range. (c) Delta alpha (higher minus lower area): mouse VISp to HVAs (green; 30 units, ranks 2-15; mean +/- 1.96 SE over 30 mice, from sci:sha256:27b767c0), macaque with the same estimator (blue) and with the main estimator (orange; mean +/- 1.96 SD over 200 draws).

Linear read-out between areas. (a) rho = FEV of the higher area from a lower-area predictor divided by FEV of held-out lower-area units (orange); rho_rev = the reverse (blue). FEV is noise-corrected; predictors and targets use disjoint repeat thirds. V1 to V2 rho_rev intervals exceed the axis because FEV of V2 from V2 is about 0.07. (b) Delta alpha of the lower-area-predicted part and of the residual part.

Invariance without compression. (a) Class share of reliable variance (between texture families or objects; random-effects components from independent repeat halves) in the lower (blue) and higher (orange) area. (b) Delta alpha for all reliable variance (orange) and for within-class variance only (blue). Intervals: mean +/- 1.96 SD over 200 draws.

citations.reason: We use its per-mouse alpha tables as the mouse reference and test whether its within-animal hierarchy compression generalizes to macaque; it does not in these data.
Source finding of steeper spectra in higher mouse areas; our macaque data do not show it for V1-V2 or V4-IT.
Same cvPCA estimator, unit normalization and half-sample intervals.
Mouse natural-image compression on shared HVA axes; open question of mechanism that we test.
Mouse grating phase-averaged compression, related to invariance.
Noise-corrected FEV and cross-fitted part spectra; its mouse read-out result is compared with our V4-IT read-out.
Source URLs of the assemblies; SHA-256 in files/provenance/shared_datasets_used.tsv.
